units: a thick wool jacket soaks up water in a downpour
the wet cloth weighs on the shoulders and pulls the sleeves out of shape
the lining holds the damp for the whole evening
workshops spread a warm wax over the outer surface
the wax closes the tiny gaps without stopping the fibre from breathing
a thin membrane can be set between the wool and the lining
that film lets the vapour off the back escape and turns away the drops
the treated garment keeps its softness and its cut
brushing followed by a fresh coat of wax extends the protection
text: A heavy wool jacket drinks a downpour without a sound, and then it sits on the shoulders like a wet sponge. The cloth swells, the sleeves lose their shape, and the lining hangs on to the damp for the rest of the evening. Workshops looked for an answer that would not ruin the fibre. They spread a fine wax over the outer face, warm enough to sink in, and it closes the tiny gaps without smothering the cloth. Rain stays out, yet the jacket still breathes. Another route is to slip a thin membrane between the wool and the lining. That film lets the vapour off the back escape and turns away the drops arriving from outside. The garment keeps its soft fall, its clean cut and its comfort. Regular care stretches the effect: brush the surface, lay on fresh wax, and the protection holds for a whole season.

units: the speaker finds the choice between natural fibre and manufactured fibre a badly framed question
fine wool warms without adding weight
wool takes up sweat and releases it without smell
wool forms little balls when it rubs against a bag
manufactured fibre dries quickly and stands up to scuffing
manufactured fibre clings to the skin as soon as you exert yourself
a loose knit forgives a large meal and takes layers underneath
a tight top draws the outline of the body and demands an exact size
the speaker keeps both options and decides according to the use
text: People keep asking me whether to pick a natural knit or a manufactured fibre, and I think the question is framed wrongly from the start. The two families are not promising the same thing. Fine wool warms you without weight, it takes up the sweat off your back and gives it away again with no smell; against that, it pills the moment it rubs on a bag strap. A manufactured fibre dries fast and shrugs off scuffing, but it clings to the skin as soon as you push yourself. Look at the cut as well, because a good part of the comfort really lives there and nowhere else. A loose jumper forgives a big meal and takes layers underneath; a tight top draws the outline of the body and demands an exact size. Honestly, I keep both in the wardrobe and decide by the use I have in mind, whatever the shop assistants preach.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the dyer works in a workshop with a low ceiling
she sorts her skeins before lowering them into the bath
she identifies fibres by touch
she prepares her baths from bark and roots
her baths give a deep blue or a shifting red
she records every proportion in a notebook
without those notes a successful bath could not be repeated
her customers bring her worn woollens and speckled jackets
these customers refuse to get rid of their clothes
text: In a workshop with a low ceiling, the dyer sorts her skeins before she lowers them into the bath. Her craft comes down to three moves, and she describes them without any fuss. The first is about matter: her fingers tell a silky thread from a coarse waste, and both from a combed cotton. The second is about colour: she builds her baths out of bark and roots, then draws a deep blue or a shifting red whose strength changes under the sun. The third is about memory: she writes every proportion into a stained notebook, because a bath that works is never found again by luck. Her customers bring her tired woollens, dulled scarves, jackets of speckled cloth they refuse to throw out. She promises very little, she hands back honest, straightforward colours, and that stained notebook is worth more to her than the vat itself.

units: the narrator finds a quilted coat on a modest rail
at first he thinks it lacks elegance
the following weeks contradict that first judgement
the quilting traps a layer of warm air under the rain
the high collar keeps the wind out without gripping the throat
the cloth marked by the journeys takes on a living look
at the end of winter the garment grows lighter once the layers are removed
the narrator concludes that a garment is judged by use and not on display
text: I came across this quilted coat on a modest rail one autumn evening, and I wrote it off as graceless: too thick, too well behaved, sewn for sensible people. The weeks that followed proved me wrong. Under thin rain the quilting held a layer of warm air that nothing could scatter, and my shoulder stayed dry. When the wind began to run down the narrow streets, the high collar showed its intelligence: it closed the throat without gripping it. Then came the squalls, and the cloth, creased by all those journeys, took on a living look, almost drawn by hand, which unworn cloth never shows. At the end of winter, stripped of the layers it had sheltered, it grew light again and found a straight line. I will say it plainly: a garment is not judged on a hanger, but after a season of rain, wind and repeated journeys.

units: the reader has washed a jumper that shrank
the wool fibre is covered with microscopic scales
heat lifts those scales
the churning of the machine tangles the fibres together
tangled fibres cannot return to their original position
the shrinking is therefore beyond repair
washing must be done in cold water without a fierce spin
drying must be done flat on a towel
a rinse with vinegar added softens the knit
text: Dear neighbour, you asked what happened to your jumper, and the answer is purely mechanical. A wool fibre is not smooth: it carries tiny scales all along it, set and overlapping like roof tiles. Hot water lifts those scales away from the shaft. The drum then pushes the fibres against one another, over and over, and the raised edges catch on each other like little hooks. The knit tightens, the surface goes hard and boardy, and the garment loses a whole size. No amount of ironing will undo that tangle, since the scales stay locked into each other for good. With the next piece, wash it in cold water, spin it gently if you spin it at all, and dry it flat on a thick towel. A final rinse with a splash of vinegar softens the knit again and gives it back the easy fall it had at the start. Love from me.

units: the question is whether to give up fine knits because they pill
pilling comes from short fibres that work their way to the surface
rubbing rolls those fibres into little balls
a long twisted yarn cuts this fault down sharply
the garment must be turned inside out before washing
loads mixing in rough materials should be avoided
a fabric shaver lifts the balls without digging into the knit
the jumper must be stored folded and not hung up
a well treated garment holds up over many long seasons
text: Should fine knits be given up simply because they pill? The answer calls for a distinction. The fault begins with short fibres that work their way to the surface, and rubbing then rolls them into tight little balls. A long, well twisted yarn cuts that down sharply, and the composition label tells you more about it than the look of the garment or the price on display. What can be done with a piece already affected? Turn it inside out before washing, keep it out of loads that mix in rough materials, and run a fabric shaver over it, which lifts the balls without digging into the knit. Should storage change as well? It should: a close-fitting jumper sags at the shoulders as soon as it hangs, so it belongs folded flat. Handled that way, a fine woollen lasts many long seasons without drooping or dulling.

units: a customer hesitates between two jackets
the fitted cut flatters him but hampers the movement of his arms
the wide cut leaves freedom of movement
the customer fears the wide cut will make him look scruffy
the assistant advises taking the intended use into account
the fitted jacket suits meetings and sit-down meals
the wide jacket suits moving about and carrying bags
the assistant offers to take in the shoulders of the wide jacket
the customer leaves with the wide jacket after that offer
text: The customer stood between two jackets hanging side by side on the rail and set out his difficulty straight away. The fitted cut, he said, flattered him, and yet it locked his arm the moment he reached towards a shelf. The wide cut gave him back his freedom, at the risk of making him look scruffy. The assistant listened, then offered a useful comparison. The first jacket, she said, suits meetings and sit-down meals, where you move little and the outline counts. The second goes with moving about, with journeys spent on your feet, with bags carried on the shoulder. She added that a small alteration at the shoulders would tighten the second one without taking away its ease. The customer thought it over for a moment, then walked out with the wide jacket and the alteration agreed.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first cloths come from stalks soaked in water
these stalks give a cool fibre that creases easily
the taming of flocks supplies a warm and springy fibre
spinning this fibre is learnt from childhood
a shining thread is obtained from unwound cocoons
this shining thread travels over long distances
a downy plant capsule gives a washable and cheap cloth
looms then produce a ribbed velvet
each new material has changed the ordinary wardrobe
text: Have you ever wondered where the cloth we wear comes from? Let us go through them family by family, without hurrying. The oldest of them come out of stalks left to soak in water, beaten and then combed: from that comes a cool fibre, pleasant in warm weather, which creases at the slightest movement. Next comes the fleece of tamed flocks, warm and springy, spun in the home by hands trained from childhood on. Later a shining thread appears, unwound from cocoons, light enough to carry along endless roads and dear enough to be kept for formal dress alone. A downy plant capsule finally gives a washable cloth, cheap to make, dressing whole populations. Improved looms add corduroy in their turn, a thick ribbed velvet. Every one of these materials has redrawn the ordinary wardrobe in its own way.

units: the fleece is taken off the animal in one piece
a wash removes the grease and the dust
carding pulls the fibres apart and lays them in one direction
twisting turns the ribbon of fibres into strong yarn
the yarn is then stretched on a loom to form a cloth
dyeing can be done on the yarn or on the finished cloth
milling in water draws the cloth together and makes it denser
cutting and stitching complete the making of the garment
text: It all starts in a sheep shed, when the shearer takes the whole fleece off in one piece. That greasy mass goes into the wash: the grease and the dust are rinsed away, the twigs are picked out, and the wool is spread to dry. Then comes carding, which pulls the tangled strands apart and lays them in a single direction. The ribbon that results goes to the wheel or the machine, where twist turns it into strong yarn. The yarn is stretched on a loom, crossed patiently with a second, and an even cloth grows steadily under the weaver's hands. Dyeing happens at this stage, or much earlier, on the bare yarn. A milling in warm water then draws the fibres closer and makes the surface denser, softer under the hand. Cutting and stitching finish the long passage from the animal to the garment worn.

units: the night watchman wears a badly worn coat
he lends this coat to an apprentice who is shivering
the apprentice discovers a lining sewn by hand
the lining holds embroidered initials and a hidden pocket
the pocket contains a piece of shining cloth
the watchman explains that this piece comes from his mother's dress
the apprentice has the coat mended by a seamstress
the watchman accepts the repair but refuses a replacement garment
text: The night watchman's coat was worn through at the elbows, and that had never troubled the man who owned it. An apprentice stood shivering outside the empty warehouse, her hands under her arms, and he held it out to her without a word of explanation. As she pulled it closed she felt a lining sewn by hand, with initials embroidered in dark thread and a pocket hidden under the seam. Inside it she found a square of silky cloth, glossy, soft as still water against her frozen fingers. The watchman said at last that the square came from a dress his mother had worn, and that he had tucked it there to keep it on him. The apprentice took the coat to a seamstress, who rebuilt the elbows and strengthened the sleeves. The watchman accepted the repair. He flatly refused the replacement coat he was offered afterwards.
